statements.quote: Mark might end up a real, actual Saint in the bedeviled hellscape of American Healthcare.
statements.context: 2024 preface to a republished satirical piece. The author apologizes to Mark Cuban and the Cost Plus Drugs team, says he under-appreciated the strategy, and expects Cuban's Cost Plus Drug Company may end up a real force for good ('Saint') in American healthcare, meaning it succeeds at cutting drug costs.
entities: Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC)
statements.note: Metaphorical 'Saint' = Cost Plus Drugs succeeds at lowering drug costs. Preface written 2024, reverses the 2022 satire's stance.

statements.quote: The piece is written as satire, but, in retrospect, I may end up agreeing with the satire as reality, which is probably what I get for being snarky.
statements.context: 2024 preface. The author expects he may come to agree that the satirical premise (Mark Cuban as a saint of drug pricing) is literally true.
entities: Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC)
statements.note: Borderline: concerns the author's own future opinion rather than an external state of the world. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: That workaround allows insane markups, hidden from the rest of us and buried in our insurance premiums, to continue for even longer.
statements.context: Closing of the satirical 2022 piece (Book 7: Genesis). The author argues Cost Plus Drugs' cash-pay workaround lets PBM/insurer markups hidden in insurance premiums persist longer, rather than fixing the system.
entities: Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC)
statements.note: Inside a satirical piece but the claim reads as sincere. The 2024 preface partly retracts the piece ('I was Wrong').

statements.quote: What comes next is the first of a five-part epic on Lithium monitoring.
statements.context: The author's intro to a guest series by 'Alex' (a physicist). Announces the newsletter will publish five parts on lithium monitoring.
statements.note: Publication plan for the author's own newsletter (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: United Healthcare provides so much money to politicians in Congress! Enforcement actions against it will never ever make a change in behavior— or a dent in it’s remarkable profits.
statements.context: After describing United/Optum mass layoffs in Texas and Florida and possible WARN Act violations, the author asserts that enforcement actions (WARN Act, DOJ) will never change UnitedHealth's behavior or dent its profits.
statements.note: Reinforced by 'Any fine, however large, is a rounding error.'

statements.quote: The remarkable thing about United Healthcare? It gets away with behavior that is going to harm more of us—and more profoundly—than the opioid crisis.
statements.context: Comparing UnitedHealth to big oil, big tobacco and Purdue Pharma, the author predicts United's conduct will harm more Americans, more profoundly, than the opioid crisis; cites the Change Healthcare cyberattack as an example.
statements.note: Comparative harm claim; hard to resolve but a sincere forward-looking call.

statements.quote: As many of you all are aware with Project Monarch, we've completed 15 consolidations. To date, we have 12 additional consolidations remaining to be completed through early 2025.
statements.context: Verbatim transcript of a United/Optum management call on 2024-07-18 to surviving employees in the North Texas market: the clinic footprint is being consolidated from 108 to 77 clinics, with 12 more consolidations to be completed through early 2025.
statements.note: Quoted third party (United management); the author reports it and does not adopt it.

statements.quote: My role was on the palliative care team and we are abandoning the most fragile and vulnerable seniors/ disabled. I’m disgusted with how this rolled out. My home bound patients will suffer.
statements.context: Unverified report from a laid-off United employee in the Gulf Coast market (600+ social workers cut, home and community based services division shut down); the source predicts home-bound patients will suffer.
statements.note: Quoted third party (anonymous laid-off employee), flagged by the author as unverified; not adopted by the author.

statements.quote: And while it has been my intention to seek daily-cadence publication, I believe it is in the best interest of my readers and the country for me to stand down and to focus solely on fulfilling my duties as Editor of this newsletter for the remainder of this article.
statements.context: Parody of Biden's 2024 withdrawal speech. The author announces he will stop daily authorship of The Frontier Psychiatrists and step back to an editor role.
statements.note: Satirical format with a punchline ('for the remainder of this article'), but the cadence change itself reads as sincere (the next post refers to 'my prior announcement about stepping down from a daily cadence').

statements.quote: I will speak to my readers later this week in more detail about my decision and the cadence at which this newsletter will continue.
statements.context: Same parody announcement. The author says he will publish more detail later this week on the newsletter's future cadence.
statements.note: Own-newsletter plan (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: This might end up as the new cover for my book. What do we think?
statements.context: The author's intro to guest part IV; refers to an image that might become the new cover of his book Inessential Pharmacology.
statements.note: Trivial own-product statement, half a question; logged for recall.

statements.quote: The 2025 physician fee schedule has an open comment period. I’m excited to encourage perusal and open comments, and I'll post more soon.
statements.context: 'Updates' list at the end of the lithium series conclusion. The author says he will post more soon about the CMS 2025 physician fee schedule open comment period.
statements.note: Own-newsletter plan tied to a payer-policy topic (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment 2025 is coming in January!
statements.context: 'Updates' list. The author announces that the Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment (RAMHT) 2025 conference will take place in January 2025.
statements.note: Author's own conference (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: Both groups will use the BrainsWay Deep TMS Device. There will be no sham or placebo treatments.
statements.context: Recruitment notice for Fermata.health's non-inferiority trial (NCT06357832) comparing once-daily H1 Deep TMS with an investigational multiple-daily H1 iTBS protocol for treatment-resistant depression in Brooklyn; states how the trial will be run.
statements.note: Trial-design statement for the author's own company (CONTROL candidate); quote joins two adjacent sentences.

statements.quote: This column is a think—or maybe feel?— piece on the (soon-to-be decided) MDMA-AT FDA submission
statements.context: The author's intro to a guest column by Alison McInnes on the MAPS/Lykos MDMA-assisted therapy application after the negative ICER review and FDA AdComm vote; he describes the FDA decision as coming soon.
statements.note: Timing-only call (FDA will decide soon); no direction stated. The guest's 'I hope ... MDMA-AT ends up being approved' is a wish and is not logged.

statements.quote: I don't mean their companies. I mean, employers—the humans—will be held personally liable for a very expensive issue.
statements.context: Opening of a piece on ERISA fiduciary-duty class actions over employee health benefits (Wells Fargo, Johnson & Johnson, Mayo Clinic). The author predicts individual employers/plan committee members will be held personally liable, with no meaningful D&O insurance protection, for almost every private employer in America.
statements.note: Restates an earlier newsletter call that a legal change would lead to a firestorm of litigation.

statements.quote: This firestorm? Employee Health Benefits. This, by the way, isn’t an accident. It’s a plan by evangelicals in the self-funded employer space. It will destroy Big Health as we know it.
statements.context: The author predicts the wave of ERISA fiduciary lawsuits over employee health benefits, driven by self-funded-employer advocates, will destroy the large vertically integrated insurers ('Big Health': Express Scripts/Cigna, OptumRx/UnitedHealth, Caremark/CVS, CarelonRx/Elevance).
statements.note: Strong, undated call.

statements.quote: So, Wells Fargo and J+J are maybe screwed
statements.context: After quoting the Wells Fargo class action (Express Scripts/Accredo markups, Wells Fargo's own benefits-consulting statements) and Lewandowski v. J&J, the author hedges that both defendants may lose.
statements.note: Litigation-outcome call about two named defendants.

statements.quote: However, this same pattern will recur for almost every private employer in America.
statements.context: The author predicts the ERISA health-benefit fiduciary lawsuit pattern will recur for almost every private employer, because most get benefits through Big Health companies that steer premium dollars to wholly owned PBMs and pharmacies at large markups.

statements.quote: Every employee who gets annoyed with their employer, which will be many, can use this rationale to sue.
statements.context: The author expects many annoyed employees to use the fiduciary-duty rationale to sue employers, comparing it to how software piracy was weaponized against employers.
statements.note: Partly overlaps the 'most employers ... will get sued' call.

statements.quote: I'm not saying it's nice, but I am saying most employers in this country will get sued.
statements.context: Closing forecast: most US employers will be sued over health-benefit fiduciary breaches.
statements.note: Compound passage split: this is the 'will get sued' half; the 'likely going to lose' half is logged separately.

statements.quote: And they're likely going to lose, and that's going to suck.
statements.context: Continuation of the closing forecast: the sued employers will likely lose the ERISA health-benefit fiduciary cases.
statements.note: Second half of the compound closing passage.
